Diuretic therapy (furosemide).summary: Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide) are used in acute heart failure. Maximal daily i.v. dose generally considered 400–600 mg, though up to 1000 mg may be considered in patients with severely impaired kidney function. Combination therapy can add a diuretic with a different site of action (e.g., thiazides, metolazone, acetazolamide).
key_points: Typical maximal daily i.v. loop diuretic dose: 400–600 mg (may consider up to 1000 mg in severe renal impairment).
Combination therapy: add a diuretic with different site of action (thiazide, metolazone, acetazolamide).

11.3.4 Vasodilators.summary: Intravenous vasodilators (nitrates, nitroprusside) dilate venous and arterial vessels, reduce venous return and afterload, increase stroke volume and relieve symptoms. Nitrates act mainly on peripheral veins; nitroprusside is a balanced arterial and venous dilator.
indications: May be more effective than diuretics when acute pulmonary oedema is caused by increased afterload and fluid redistribution to the lungs with minimal fluid accumulation.
May be considered to relieve acute heart failure (AHF) symptoms when systolic BP (SBP) > 110 mmHg.
administration_notes: Nitrates generally given with an initial bolus followed by continuous infusion; may also be given as repeated boluses.
Nitroglycerine boluses (example dose mentioned for severely hypertensive patients with acute pulmonary oedema).
cautions: Avoid hypotension from excessive decrease in preload and afterload.
Use extreme caution in patients with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and/or severe aortic stenosis.
No clear recommendation favouring vasodilator regimen vs. usual care to date based on recent randomized trials.

11.3.5 Inotropes.summary: Inotropes are used for patients with low cardiac output and hypotension, reserved for LV systolic dysfunction with low cardiac output and low SBP (e.g., <90 mmHg) resulting in poor organ perfusion. Use with caution, start low and uptitrate with close monitoring.
indications: Patients with low cardiac output and hypotension (poor vital organ perfusion).
Reserved for LV systolic dysfunction with low SBP (example threshold <90 mmHg).
risks_and_adverse_effects: Adrenergic inotropes can cause sinus tachycardia, increased ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation, myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmias, and increased mortality.
Excessive peripheral vasodilation and hypotension can limit use of type-3-phosphodiesterase inhibitors (or levosimendan), especially at high doses or when started with a bolus.
drug_preferences_and_notes: Levosimendan or type-3-phosphodiesterase inhibitors may be preferred over dobutamine for patients on beta-blockers because they act via independent mechanisms.
Use cautiously with close haemodynamic monitoring; start at low doses and uptitrate.

11.3.6 Vasopressors.summary: Vasopressors are used for AHF patients with severe hypotension to increase perfusion to vital organs; norepinephrine may be preferred among peripheral arterial vasoconstrictors.
indications: Severe hypotension with the goal of increasing perfusion to vital organs.
considerations: Norepinephrine preferred in severe hypotension but increases LV afterload.
Combination of norepinephrine and inotropic agents may be considered, particularly in advanced heart failure and cardiogenic shock.
